1	# sd v1.0.0 — CLI argument-parsing behavior (black-box probing report)
2	
3	Binary probed: `/workspace/executable`. All probes used only its normal CLI
4	interface (args/stdin/stdout/stderr). All output captured to files and verified
5	with `od -c` where byte-exactness mattered. Commands below were run from `/tmp`;
6	unless noted, stdin was `echo "aaa aaa aaa"` (or `"aaa AAA aaa"` where case
7	mattered) piped in.
8	
9	**Overall shape:** argument parsing is unmistakably Rust **clap v4** style
10	(error wording, `tip:` lines, `Usage:` lines, exit code 2). The reimplementation
11	should reproduce these strings byte-for-byte.
12	
13	## 1. Exit codes
14	
15	| Situation | Exit code |
16	|---|---|
17	| Success (replacement done or no match) | 0 |
18	| `--help`, `-h`, `--version`, `-V` (even mixed with errors/junk) | 0 |
19	| Any argument-parse error (unknown flag, missing arg, bad value, repeated flag, unexpected value) | **2** |
20	| Runtime errors, e.g. nonexistent file: `error: invalid path: b` | 1 |
21	
22	(Man page also documents 101 for panics; not triggered in CLI parsing.)
23	
24	## 2. argv[0] / program name in output
25	
26	- The `Usage:` line uses the **basename of argv[0]**, not the fixed string `sd`.
27	  Invoked as `/workspace/executable`, every usage line says `Usage: executable ...`.
28	  After `cp /workspace/executable /tmp/mytoolname; cd /tmp; ./mytoolname --help`,
29	  the line became `Usage: mytoolname [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
30	  (invoked as `./mytoolname` — only basename appears).
31	- The help **header** is the fixed string `sd v1.0.0` (does NOT follow argv[0]).
32	- `--version` prints the fixed string `sd 1.0.0` (does NOT follow argv[0]).
33	
34	## 3. `--version` / `-V`
35	
36	- Command: `/workspace/executable --version` (and `-V`)
37	- stdout, byte-exact (`od -c`): `s d SP 1 . 0 . 0 \n` — i.e. `sd 1.0.0\n`
38	  (7 chars + newline). **No `v` prefix**, unlike the help header.
39	- stderr: empty. Exit 0.
40	- `--version` wins over everything else on the command line:
41	  - `sd a b --version` → prints version, exit 0.
42	  - `sd --version --badflag` → prints version, exit 0 (error suppressed).
43	  - In a short cluster, the FIRST of `-h`/`-V` wins: `-hV` → help; `-Vh` → version.
44	- `--version=x` → exit 2, stderr:
45	  ```
46	  error: unexpected value 'x' for '--version' found; no more were expected
47	
48	  Usage: executable --version <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
49	
50	  For more information, try '--help'.
51	  ```
52	
53	## 4. `--help` (long) — exit 0, stdout only, stderr empty
54	
55	Byte count 1394. No ANSI codes (even on a TTY — verified under `script`).
56	Exact full text (note: `Usage:` line contains argv[0] basename; shown as run
57	via `/workspace/executable`):
58	
59	```
60	sd v1.0.0
61	An intuitive find & replace CLI
62	
63	Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
64	
65	Arguments:
66	  <FIND>
67	          The regexp or string (if using `-F`) to search for
68	
69	  <REPLACE_WITH>
70	          What to replace each match with. Unless in string mode, you may use captured values like
71	          $1, $2, etc
72	
73	  [FILES]...
74	          The path to file(s). This is optional - sd can also read from STDIN.
75	          
76	          Note: sd modifies files in-place by default. See documentation for examples.
77	
78	Options:
79	  -p, --preview
80	          Display changes in a human reviewable format (the specifics of the format are likely to
81	          change in the future)
82	
83	  -F, --fixed-strings
84	          Treat FIND and REPLACE_WITH args as literal strings
85	
86	  -n, --max-replacements <LIMIT>
87	          Limit the number of replacements that can occur per file. 0 indicates unlimited
88	          replacements
89	          
90	          [default: 0]
91	
92	  -f, --flags <FLAGS>
93	          Regex flags. May be combined (like `-f mc`).
94	          
95	          c - case-sensitive
96	          
97	          e - disable multi-line matching
98	          
99	          i - case-insensitive
100	          
101	          m - multi-line matching
102	          
103	          s - make `.` match newlines
104	          
105	          w - match full words only
106	
107	  -h, --help
108	          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
109	
110	  -V, --version
111	          Print version
112	```
113	
114	Notes: description lines are indented 10 spaces; continuation lines are
115	hard-wrapped (looks like 100-column wrap); blank separator lines inside
116	`[FILES]...`, `-n`, `-f` blocks contain **10 trailing spaces** (the indent)
117	before the newline — reproduce exactly if matching bytes. File ends with a
118	single `\n`.
119	
120	## 5. `-h` (short) — DIFFERENT from `--help`, exit 0, stdout only
121	
122	Byte count 1053, no ANSI codes. Exact full text:
123	
124	```
125	sd v1.0.0
126	An intuitive find & replace CLI
127	
128	Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
129	
130	Arguments:
131	  <FIND>          The regexp or string (if using `-F`) to search for
132	  <REPLACE_WITH>  What to replace each match with. Unless in string mode, you may use captured
133	                  values like $1, $2, etc
134	  [FILES]...      The path to file(s). This is optional - sd can also read from STDIN
135	
136	Options:
137	  -p, --preview                   Display changes in a human reviewable format (the specifics of the
138	                                  format are likely to change in the future)
139	  -F, --fixed-strings             Treat FIND and REPLACE_WITH args as literal strings
140	  -n, --max-replacements <LIMIT>  Limit the number of replacements that can occur per file. 0
141	                                  indicates unlimited replacements [default: 0]
142	  -f, --flags <FLAGS>             Regex flags. May be combined (like `-f mc`).
143	  -h, --help                      Print help (see more with '--help')
144	  -V, --version                   Print version
145	```
146	
147	Differences from `--help`: one-line-per-arg layout (descriptions aligned in a
148	column, wrapped with hanging indent at column 34); `-f` description is just the
149	first line (flag list omitted); `-n` shows `[default: 0]` inline; the `-h` help
150	text itself differs (`see a summary with '-h'` vs `see more with '--help'`);
151	`[FILES]...` omits the trailing `.` and the in-place note.
152	
153	- Help wins over errors anywhere: `sd a b --help`, `sd --help --badflag` →
154	  full `--help` text, exit 0. `sd -h` anywhere → short help.
155	
156	## 6. Unknown flags
157	
158	### 6.1 Unknown long flag, no near match
159	`sd --badflag` → exit 2, stdout empty, stderr byte-exact (ends with single `\n`):
160	```
161	error: unexpected argument '--badflag' found
162	
163	  tip: to pass '--badflag' as a value, use '-- --badflag'
164	
165	Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
166	
167	For more information, try '--help'.
168	```
169	
170	### 6.2 Unknown short flag
171	`sd -Z` → exit 2:
172	```
173	error: unexpected argument '-Z' found
174	
175	  tip: to pass '-Z' as a value, use '-- -Z'
176	
177	Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
178	
179	For more information, try '--help'.
180	```
181	
182	### 6.3 Near-miss long flag → suggestion tip, and usage line CHANGES
183	`sd --previw a b`, `sd --fixd-strings a b`, `sd --max-replacement 2 a b`,
184	`sd --flag i a b` → exit 2. Example (`--previw`):
185	```
186	error: unexpected argument '--previw' found
187	
188	  tip: a similar argument exists: '--preview'
189	
190	Usage: executable <--preview|--fixed-strings|--max-replacements <LIMIT>|--flags <FLAGS>|FIND|REPLACE_WITH|FILES>
191	
192	For more information, try '--help'.
193	```
194	Note the usage line becomes an **alternation** of all option flags (long names,
195	with value placeholders) plus bare positional names, wrapped in `<...>`.
196	
197	BUT when the suggestion is `--help` or `--version`, the usage line instead
198	shows that single suggested flag inserted:
199	- `sd --vers` → tip `'--version'`, usage: `Usage: executable --version <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
200	- `sd --versoin a b` → same as `--vers`.
201	- `sd ---help a b` → `error: unexpected argument '---help' found`, tip
202	  `a similar argument exists: '--help'`, usage: `Usage: executable --help <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
203	
204	No prefix-abbreviation matching: `--vers` is NOT accepted as `--version`.
205	
206	### 6.4 TTY behavior
207	Under a pseudo-TTY (`script -qec ...`), error and help output contain **zero
208	ANSI escape sequences** (verified by scanning captured bytes for ESC). Output
209	is plain text in all modes — no color support at all.
210	
211	## 7. Missing arguments
212	
213	### 7.1 Zero args — `sd` → exit 2
214	```
215	error: the following required arguments were not provided:
216	  <FIND>
217	  <REPLACE_WITH>
218	
219	Usage: executable <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
220	
221	For more information, try '--help'.
222	```
223	Note: `[OPTIONS]` is **absent** from this usage line (vs. unknown-flag errors
224	which include it).
225	
226	### 7.2 One arg — `sd foo` → exit 2
227	Same shape, listing only `  <REPLACE_WITH>`.
228	
229	### 7.3 Usage line reflects flags already given
230	- `sd -p` (missing both positionals) → usage: `Usage: executable --preview <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
231	- `sd -f a b` (`-f` consumes `a`; then FIND=b, REPLACE_WITH missing) → usage:
232	  `Usage: executable --flags <FLAGS> <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
233	- `sd --` → same as zero args (`Usage: executable <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`).
234	
235	## 8. `-n` / `--max-replacements` (value parsed as u64)
236	
237	Accepted forms (all exit 0, limit = N replacements):
238	- `-n 2` (space), `-n2` (attached), `-n=2` (equals), `-Fn2`/`-pn2` (last in short cluster),
239	  `--max-replacements 2`, `--max-replacements=2`.
240	- Semantics: N = max matches replaced; `-n 0` = unlimited (also the default);
241	  input `aaa aaa aaa`, `sd -n 2 a b` → `bba aaa aaa`.
242	- Leading `+` accepted: `-n=+3` works (3 replacements) — consistent with Rust
243	  `u64::from_str`. Leading zeros accepted (`03`). Leading whitespace NOT
244	  trimmed: `-n " 3"` → invalid digit error. u64 max `18446744073709551615`
245	  accepted (effectively unlimited); `18446744073709551616` rejected.
246	
247	Error cases (all exit 2, stdout empty):
248	- `-n abc` / `-n 1.5` / `-n 0x3` / `-n " 3"`:
249	  ```
250	  error: invalid value 'abc' for '--max-replacements <LIMIT>': invalid digit found in string
251	
252	  For more information, try '--help'.
253	  ```
254	  (No `Usage:` line on invalid-value errors!)
255	- `-n ""` → `error: invalid value '' for '--max-replacements <LIMIT>': cannot parse integer from empty string`
256	- `-n 99999999999999999999999999` → `...: number too large to fit in target type`
257	- `-n=-1` (equals form) → `error: invalid value '-1' for '--max-replacements <LIMIT>': invalid digit found in string`
258	- `-n -1` or `--max-replacements -1` (space form): value starting with `-` is
259	  NOT consumed; `-1` is parsed as a new argument →
260	  `error: unexpected argument '-1' found` + tip `to pass '-1' as a value, use '-- -1'`
261	  + full usage line with `[OPTIONS]`.
262	- `-n` at end / `-n` followed by another flag (`-n -p a b`) →
263	  ```
264	  error: a value is required for '--max-replacements <LIMIT>' but none was supplied
265	
266	  For more information, try '--help'.
267	  ```
268	  (No usage line.)
269	- Repeated: `-n 1 -n 2` →
270	  ```
271	  error: the argument '--max-replacements <LIMIT>' cannot be used multiple times
272	
273	  Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...
274	
275	  For more information, try '--help'.
276	  ```
277	- `-n2F` → value is `2F` → invalid digit error (once `-n` takes the rest of the
278	  cluster as its value).
279	
280	## 9. `-f` / `--flags`
281	
282	Accepted forms: `-f i`, `-fi`, `-f=i`, `--flags i`, `--flags=i`, `--flags=-i`,
283	`-f=-i`, and as last element of a short cluster (`-pfi` → flags value `i`).
284	- Once `-f` appears in a cluster, the REST of the cluster is its value:
285	  `-fp` → flags value `p` (case-sensitive run; `p` is not a regex flag and is
286	  silently ignored). `-pfi2` → flags value `i2`.
287	- **Unknown/invalid flag characters are silently IGNORED** (exit 0): `-f x`,
288	  `-f zyx`, `-f ""`, `--flags=` all succeed with default (case-sensitive,
289	  multiline) behavior. No validation error exists for `-f` content at the CLI
290	  layer.
291	- `-f` without a following value (`sd a b -f`) →
292	  `error: a value is required for '--flags <FLAGS>' but none was supplied` (exit 2, no usage line).
293	- `-f` followed by a dash-arg (`-f -i a b`) → `-i` NOT consumed:
294	  `error: unexpected argument '-i' found` + tip + usage (exit 2).
295	- Repeated `-f i -f m` →
296	  `error: the argument '--flags <FLAGS>' cannot be used multiple times` + usage (exit 2).
297	
298	## 10. Repeated flags (all exit 2)
299	
300	Every flag/option is single-use; repeating any gives
301	`error: the argument '<canonical long form>' cannot be used multiple times`
302	followed by `Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...` and
303	the `For more information` line:
304	- `-p -p` → `'--preview'`
305	- `-F -F` → `'--fixed-strings'`
306	- `-n 1 -n 2` → `'--max-replacements <LIMIT>'`
307	- `-f i -f m` → `'--flags <FLAGS>'`
308	
309	## 11. Combined short flags
310	
311	- `-pF`, `-Fp` → both set, exit 0.
312	- `-Fn 2`, `-Fn2`, `-pn2` → work; value-taking flag must be last in cluster.
313	- `-hV` → help (first wins); `-Vh` → version.
314	- `-pf i` / `-pfi` → `-f` takes `i` (rest of cluster or next arg).
315	
316	## 12. Flags after positional args
317	
318	Flags are recognized ANYWHERE (no positional/flag ordering requirement):
319	- `sd a b -F`, `sd a b -p` → flags applied, exit 0.
320	- `sd a b --help` → help, exit 0; `sd a b --version` → version, exit 0.
321	
322	## 13. `--` separator
323	
324	- Everything after `--` is positional, even dash-leading:
325	  `sd -- -F -w` → FIND=`-F`, REPLACE_WITH=`-w`; `echo "./hello --foo" | sd -- "--foo" "-w"` → `./hello -w` (matches README).
326	- `sd -- --help x` → FIND=`--help` (literal), exit 0.
327	- `sd a -- -F` → replace-with = `-F` (works).
328	- `sd a b -- -d` → `-d` treated as a FILE → runtime error
329	  `error: invalid path: -d`, exit **1**.
330	- `sd --` alone → same missing-args error as zero args (exit 2).
331	- README's claim is confirmed: without `--`, `sd "foo" "-w"` fails with
332	  `error: unexpected argument '-w' found ...` exit 2.
333	
334	## 14. Miscellaneous
335	
336	- A lone `-` is a POSITIONAL value, not a flag: `sd - a b` → FIND=`-`,
337	  REPLACE_WITH=`a`, FILES=[`b`] → `error: invalid path: b`, exit 1.
338	- Boolean long flags reject values: `--fixed-strings=x` →
339	  `error: unexpected value 'x' for '--fixed-strings' found; no more were expected`
340	  + `Usage: executable --fixed-strings <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...` (exit 2);
341	  `--preview=true` analogous; `--help=x`, `--version=x` analogous.
342	- Empty FIND is allowed at CLI level (`sd "" b` runs fine, replaces empty matches).
343	- All parse-error messages: stdout is always empty; everything goes to stderr;
344	  every message ends with exactly one trailing `\n`.
345	- Runtime errors (invalid path) print `error: invalid path: <path>\n` to stderr,
346	  exit 1 — distinct from parse errors (exit 2).
347	
348	## 15. Reimplementation checklist (exact templates)
349	
350	Usage line base: `Usage: {argv0_basename} [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...`
351	(with `[OPTIONS]` omitted or replaced by specific flags in some error contexts —
352	see §6.3, §7, §14).
353	
354	Error trailer (when usage shown):
355	`\nFor more information, try '--help'.\n` preceded by a blank line after the
356	usage line. Invalid-value and value-required errors have NO usage line — just
357	the error line, blank line, and the `For more information` line.
358	
359	Parse errors → exit 2. Help/version → exit 0, stdout. Runtime file errors →
360	exit 1. No ANSI color ever.

1	# sd v1.0.0 — Replacement Template Semantics (black-box probing report)
2	
3	Binary: `/workspace/executable`. All probes used stdin/stdout only (no file args).
4	Unless noted otherwise, input was fed with `printf '%s'` (NO trailing newline), so the
5	`od -c` dumps below show the exact output bytes with no ambiguity about trailing newlines.
6	"regex mode" = default; "`-F` mode" = `--fixed-strings`.
7	
8	Harness used for most probes (records exact bytes + exit code):
9	
10	```bash
11	printf '%s' "$INPUT" | /workspace/executable <args...> >/tmp/out 2>/tmp/err; echo $?
12	od -c /tmp/out; od -c /tmp/err
13	```
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Two completely different replacement modes
18	
19	- **Regex mode (default):** replacement is a template: `$$` escapes, `$`-group
20	  references, AND backslash-escape unescaping (`\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\xNN`) all apply.
21	- **`-F` mode:** replacement is 100% literal. No `$$` escape, no `$1` interpolation,
22	  no backslash unescaping. Nothing is special.
23	
24	Evidence (`-F`):
25	
26	```
27	$ printf 'a$1b' | ./executable -F '$1' '[$1]'   → stdout: a[$1]b        exit 0
28	$ printf 'a$1b' | ./executable -F 'a' '$$'      → stdout: $$$1b         exit 0   (literal $$)
29	$ printf 'a(x)b' | ./executable -F '(x)' '$name' → stdout: a$nameb      exit 0
30	$ printf 'aNb'   | ./executable -F 'N' 'P\nQ'   → stdout: aP\nQb        exit 0   (literal backslash-n)
31	$ printf 'foo'   | ./executable -F 'foo' '$1x'  → stdout: $1x           exit 0   (no ambiguity check!)
32	```
33	
34	Everything in sections 2–8 below applies to **regex mode only**.
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 2. Numbered group references: `$0`, `$1`..`$N`, `${N}`
39	
40	- `$1`..`$9`, `$10`, `$12`… all work; the reference consumes the **longest run of
41	  ASCII digits** after `$`.
42	- `$0` / `${0}` = whole match.
43	- Leading zeros are fine: `$01`, `$001` both refer to group 1.
44	- Out-of-range indexes (incl. `$5` with 2 groups, `$10` with 2 groups, `$99`,
45	  `$1` with zero groups in the pattern) expand to **empty string, silently, exit 0**.
46	  There is NO error for nonexistent numbered groups.
47	
48	```
49	$ printf 'abc123def456' | ./executable '([a-z]+)([0-9]+)' '$1|$2|$1'
50	  → abc|123|abcdef|456|def                                exit 0
51	$ printf 'abc123' | ./executable '([a-z]+)([0-9]+)' '[$0][$1][$2]'
52	  → [abc123][abc][123]                                    exit 0
53	$ printf 'abc123' | ./executable '([a-z]+)([0-9]+)' '[$01][$001]'
54	  → [abc][abc]                                            exit 0
55	$ printf 'abcdefghijkl' | ./executable '(a)(b)(c)(d)(e)(f)(g)(h)(i)(j)(k)(l)' '[$10][$11][$12]'
56	  → [j][k][l]                                             exit 0
57	$ printf 'abc123' | ./executable '([a-z]+)([0-9]+)' '[$5]'    → []      exit 0
58	$ printf 'abc123' | ./executable '([a-z]+)([0-9]+)' '[$10]'   → []      exit 0
59	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' '[$1]'                → []      exit 0
60	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable '(f)' '[$99]'               → []oo    exit 0
61	```
62	
63	Named groups are also addressable by number: pattern `(?P<a>x)` with `[$1][${1}]`
64	→ `[x][x]`.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## 3. Named group references: `$name`, `${name}`
69	
70	- Both `(?P<name>...)` and `(?<name>...)` work in the pattern.
71	- Name characters are **ASCII `[A-Za-z0-9_]` only** — the longest run of those after
72	  `$` is the name. `.`, `[`, `]`, `-`, space, non-ASCII (e.g. `é`) TERMINATE the name
73	  and are emitted literally.
74	- Names are **case-sensitive** (`$Dollars` ≠ `$dollars`).
75	- Longest-name matching: `$dollars_dollars` looks up the name `dollars_dollars`
76	  (which doesn't exist → empty), NOT `$dollars` + `_dollars`. Use `${dollars}_dollars`.
77	- Unknown names (with or without braces, incl. `${1x}`, `${foo}`, `${}`) expand to
78	  **empty string, silently, exit 0**.
79	
80	```
81	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '$dollars dollars and $cents cents'
82	  → 123 dollars and 45 cents                              exit 0
83	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?<dollars>\d+)\.(?<cents>\d+)' '$dollars|$cents'
84	  → 123|45                                                exit 0
85	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '${dollars}|${cents}'
86	  → 123|45                                                exit 0
87	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '$dollars_dollars and $cents_cents'
88	  →  and                            (leading space!)      exit 0
89	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '${dollars}_dollars and ${cents}_cents'
90	  → 123_dollars and 45_cents                              exit 0
91	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '[$dollars.x]'
92	  → [123.x]                  (. not part of name)         exit 0
93	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)\.(?P<cents>\d+)' '[$dollars[0]]'
94	  → [123[0]]                 ([ ] not part of name)       exit 0
95	$ printf '123' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)' '[$Dollars][$dollars]'
96	  → [][123]                  (case-sensitive)             exit 0
97	$ printf 'ab'  | ./executable '(?P<dollars>a)(b)' '[$dollarsé]'
98	  → [aé]                       (é not part of name)       exit 0
99	$ printf '123.45' | ./executable '(?P<dollars>\d+)' '${foo}'
100	  → .                          (unknown braced name → empty; '.' is leftover input)  exit 0
101	```
102	
103	---
104	
105	## 4. Groups that did not participate in the match
106	
107	Optional groups that didn't match expand to **empty string**, no error:
108	
109	```
110	$ printf 'bxc' | ./executable '(a)?b(x)c' '[$1][$2]'        → [][x]    exit 0
111	$ printf 'ac'  | ./executable '(?P<a>x)?a(?P<b>y)?c' '[$a][$b]' → [][]   exit 0
112	```

115	
116	## 5. `$$` escaping and lone-`$` cases
117	
118	- `$$` → literal `$`. This is the ONLY way to escape `$`.
119	- `$$1` → literal `$1` (the `1` is NOT a group ref — `$$` consumes both dollars,
120	  remaining chars are literal).
121	- `$$$$` → `$$`. `$$$1` → `$` + group-1 value.
122	- `$` at end of replacement → literal `$`.
123	- `$` followed by any non-name char (space, `-`, `.`, `]`, `}`, `(`, …) → literal `$`
124	  followed by that char.
125	- `${` with no closing `}` (even at end of string) → **literal `${`** (no error).
126	- `${}` (empty braces) → empty (unknown empty name).
127	- `$1.` / `$1-` / `$1 ` / `$1[` / `$1]` → group 1 then the literal char (`.`/`[`/`]`
128	  do NOT extend the reference and do NOT trigger the ambiguity error of §6).
129	
130	```
131	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' '$$bar'        → $bar         exit 0
132	$ printf 'foo bar' | ./executable '(foo)' '$$1'        → $1 bar        exit 0
133	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'o' '$$$$'           → f$$$$         exit 0
134	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable '(foo)' '$$$1'       → $foo          exit 0
135	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'end$'         → end$          exit 0
136	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a$ b'         → a$ b          exit 0
137	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a$-b'         → a$-b          exit 0
138	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a$.b'         → a$.b          exit 0
139	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a${b'         → a${b          exit 0
140	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a${'          → a${           exit 0
141	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable 'foo' 'a${}b'        → ab            exit 0
142	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable '(foo)' '[$1.]'      → [foo.]        exit 0
143	$ printf 'foo'     | ./executable '(foo)' '[$1-]'      → [foo-]        exit 0
144	$ printf 'ab'      | ./executable '(a)(b)' '[$1[][$1]]' → [a[][a]]     exit 0
145	```
146	
147	---
148	
149	## 6. THE ambiguity error (numbered ref followed by a word char) — exact spec
150	
151	**Trigger:** in regex mode, a `$` (not part of a `$$` pair) followed by one or more
152	ASCII digits, IMMEDIATELY followed by an ASCII word char `[A-Za-z0-9_]`.
153	Examples that error: `$1x`, `$1_`, `$2y2`, `$10x`, `$0x`, `$01x`, `\$1x`, `\x41$1x`,
154	`A\n$1x` (raw text). Examples that do NOT: `$1.`, `$1-`, `$1 `, `$1[`, `$1é` (é is
155	non-ASCII), `$10` (pure digits at end/non-word char), `$$1x` (escaped).
156	
157	**Properties:**
158	- Exit code **1**. Stdout empty. Message on stderr.
159	- Validated UP FRONT: fires even if the pattern never matches, and even when the
160	  regex itself is invalid (`./executable '(' '$1x'` gives the ambiguity error, not a
161	  regex error) — replacement validation precedes regex compilation.
162	- Only the FIRST ambiguity is reported when several exist.
163	- Runs on the RAW replacement text (before backslash-unescaping): `\x41$1x` errors
164	  even though unescaping would swallow the `$`. The only escape it understands is `$$`.
165	- No ANSI color codes anywhere, even when stderr is a TTY (verified via `script -qec`
166	  under a pty — output identical, only `\r\n` line endings from the pty).
167	- Does NOT apply in `-F` mode (`-F foo '$1x'` → literal `$1x`, exit 0).
168	
169	**Exact stderr format** (example `printf 'abc' | ./executable '(a)(b)' '[$1x]'`):
170	
171	```
172	error: The numbered capture group `$1` in the replacement text is ambiguous.
173	hint: Use curly braces to disambiguate it `${1}x`.
174	[$1x]
175	  ^^
176	```
177	
178	Exact bytes (od -c of stderr):
179	
180	```
181	e r r o r :   T h e   n u m b e r e d   c a p t u r e   g r o u p   ` $ 1 `   i n   t h e   r e p l a c e m e n t   t e x t   i s   a m b i g u o u s . \n
182	h i n t :   U s e   c u r l y   b r a c e s   t o   d i s a m b i g u a t e   i t   ` $ { 1 } x ` . \n
183	[ $ 1 x ] \n
184	    ^ ^ \n          (2 spaces, then one caret per char of the NAME)
185	```
186	
187	Format rules:
188	- Line 1: ``error: The numbered capture group `$<digits>` in the replacement text is ambiguous.\n``
189	  where `<digits>` is the digit run only (`$1`, `$10`, `$0`, `$01`).
190	- Line 2: ``hint: Use curly braces to disambiguate it `${<digits>}<rest>`.\n``
191	  where `<rest>` is the trailing word chars (`${1}x`, `${2}y2`, `${0}x`, `${01}x`).
192	- Line 3: the full RAW replacement text + `\n`.
193	- Line 4: spaces up to the first char after the `$`, then one `^` per character of the
194	  full name (digits + trailing word chars) + `\n`. I.e. the underline spans exactly
195	  the name portion, not including the `$`.
196	
197	More examples (stderr shown via `cat -A`, `$` = end of line):
198	
199	```
200	replacement 'x$1yz'  →  hint `${1}yz`,  source line `x$1yz$`,  caret line `  ^^^$`
201	replacement '$0x'    →  group `$0`, hint `${0}x`,  source `$0x$`,  carets ` ^^$`
202	replacement '[$2y2]' →  group `$2`, hint `${2}y2`,  source `[$2y2]$`,  carets `  ^^^$`
203	replacement '$01x'   →  group `$01`, hint `${01}x`, source `$01x$`,  carets ` ^^^$`
204	```
205	
206	Valid disambiguation confirmed working:
207	
208	```
209	$ printf 'foo' | ./executable '(f)(o)(o)' '${1}x${2}y${3}z'   → fxoyoz   exit 0
210	```
211	
212	---
213	
214	## 7. Backslash escapes in the replacement (regex mode ONLY)
215	
216	The replacement template is **backslash-unescaped** before interpolation. Recognized:
217	
218	| input  | output        | notes                                        |
219	|--------|---------------|----------------------------------------------|
220	| `\n`   | LF (0x0A)     |                                              |
221	| `\t`   | TAB (0x09)    |                                              |
222	| `\r`   | CR (0x0D)     |                                              |
223	| `\\`   | `\`           |                                              |
224	| `\xNN` | char U+00NN   | exactly 2 hex digits; see BUG below          |
225	
226	- `\xNN` needs exactly two hex digits: `\x4` and `\xZZ` stay literal (`\x4`, `\xZZ`).
227	- `\xff` → the Unicode codepoint U+00FF, UTF-8 encoded (`303 277` = `ÿ`), NOT a raw byte.
228	- `\x00` → NUL byte (0x00) in output.
229	- **BUG (quirk to reproduce):** after a successful `\xNN` escape, the NEXT character
230	  of the template is silently swallowed:
231	  - `A\x41Z` → `AA` (Z gone)
232	  - `\x4141` → `A1` (first `4` of the tail gone)
233	  - `\x41XYZ` → `AYZ`
234	  - `\x41$1`  → `A1` — the `$` is swallowed, so `$1` never interpolates (with
235	    pattern `(a)(b)` on input `ab`)
236	- Unrecognized escapes keep BOTH chars literally: `\0`→`\0`, `\a`→`\a`, `\f`→`\f`,
237	  `\v`→`\v`, `\q`→`\q`, `\(`→`\(`, `\u{41}`→`\u{41}`, `\1`→`\1`.
238	- A trailing lone `\` at end of replacement stays a literal `\`.
239	- **`\$` is NOT an escape.** `\$1` → `\` + interpolated group 1 (e.g. `\X`).
240	  Likewise `A\$B` → `A\` (`\` literal, `$B` = unknown name → empty).
241	- **Order of operations:** (1) ambiguity check on raw text (§6) → (2) backslash
242	  unescape → (3) `$`-interpolation per match. Proven by `\x41$1`→`A1` and by
243	  `\x41$1x` still raising the raw-text ambiguity error.
244	- **Captured text is inserted literally** — never re-unescaped and never
245	  re-interpolated:
246	  - `printf 'a$bz' | ./executable '(\$b)' '<$1>'` → `a<$b>z`
247	  - `printf 'a\nb' | ./executable '(\\n)' '<$1>'` → `a<\n>b` (literal backslash-n kept)
248	
249	```
250	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\tB'      → A<TAB>B      exit 0
251	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\rB'      → A<CR>B       exit 0
252	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\\B'      → A\B          exit 0
253	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\nB'      → A<LF>B       exit 0
254	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' '\x41'      → A            exit 0
255	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' '\x7a'      → z            exit 0
256	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\x00B'    → A<NUL>       exit 0  (B swallowed)
257	$ printf 'X' | ./executable 'X' 'A\'        → A\           exit 0
258	$ printf 'hello' | ./executable 'l' $'N\nT\tB\\E'
259	  → heN<LF>T<TAB>B\EN<LF>T<TAB>B\Eo   (real control bytes pass through untouched)  exit 0
260	```
261	
262	---
263	
264	## 8. Empty replacement / empty matches
265	
266	- Empty replacement `''` deletes matches: `printf 'hello' | ./executable 'l' ''` → `heo`, exit 0.
267	- Patterns that match the empty string replace at every position (Rust-regex
268	  semantics): `printf 'abc' | ./executable 'x*' '[$0]'` → `[]a[]b[]c[]`, exit 0.
269	  Group refs in empty matches expand empty: `'(x)*' '<$1>'` on `abc` → `<>a<>b<>c<>`.
270	- `^` anchor: `printf 'abc' | ./executable '^' 'S>'` → `S>abc`, exit 0.
271	- Newlines/tabs/backslashes already present as real bytes in the replacement argument
272	  are passed through byte-for-byte.
273	
274	---
275	
276	## 9. Condensed grammar of the replacement template (regex mode)
277	
278	```
279	template  := chunk*
280	chunk     := '$$'                    → literal '$'
281	           | '$' name                → group lookup (empty if unknown/non-participating)
282	           | '$'                     → literal '$' (if not followed by name char / '{')
283	           | '${' name '}'           → group lookup
284	           | '${' (no closing '}')   → literal '${'
285	           | '\' ('n'|'t'|'r'|'\')   → LF/TAB/CR/backslash
286	           | '\x' HEXDIG HEXDIG      → char(codepoint) + SWALLOW next char (bug)
287	           | '\' <other>             → literal '\' + char
288	name      := [A-Za-z0-9_]+           (digits-only → numbered, else named; numbered+wordchar → AMBIGUITY ERROR)
289	```
290	
291	Validation order at startup: replacement ambiguity check FIRST (on raw text), then
292	regex compilation. Interpolation-time lookups never fail.
293	
294	---
295	
296	## 10. Ten most surprising/important findings (summary)
297	
298	1. Unknown/nonexistent references NEVER error: `$5` with 2 groups, `$99`, `$name`,
299	   `${foo}`, `${}` all expand to empty string, exit 0.
300	2. The ONLY replacement error is the "ambiguous" one: `$<digits>` immediately followed
301	   by `[A-Za-z0-9_]` → exit 1, exact message `error: The numbered capture group \`$N\` in
302	   the replacement text is ambiguous.\nhint: Use curly braces to disambiguate it \`${N}rest\`.\n`
303	   + raw replacement line + caret line underlining just the name (not the `$`).
304	3. The ambiguity check runs on the RAW text before anything else — it beats invalid-regex
305	   errors, fires with zero matches, reports only the first offender, and even fires for
306	   `\x41$1x` where unescaping would have deleted the `$`. Only `$$` is honored by it.
307	4. The replacement is backslash-unescaped in regex mode: `\n`→LF, `\t`→TAB, `\r`→CR,
308	   `\\`→`\`, `\xNN`→U+00NN (UTF-8 encoded); unknown escapes stay literal; `\$` is NOT
309	   an escape (`\$1` = `\` + group 1).
310	5. Bug to reproduce: a successful `\xNN` escape swallows the next template character
311	   (`A\x41Z`→`AA`, `\x41$1`→`A1` killing the interpolation).
312	6. Name charset is strictly ASCII `[A-Za-z0-9_]`; `.[]-` and non-ASCII terminate names;
313	   longest-name wins (`$dollars_dollars` → unknown → empty); names are case-sensitive.
314	7. `$0`/`${0}` = whole match; leading zeros OK (`$01` = group 1); numbered refs take the
315	   longest digit run (`$12` = group 12); named groups are also reachable by index.
316	8. `$$` is the only `$` escape; `$$1`→literal `$1`; unclosed `${` is literal; `$` before
317	   any non-word char or at end is literal.
318	9. `-F` mode makes the replacement fully literal — no `$$`, no `$1`, no `\n` unescaping,
319	   no ambiguity validation at all.
320	10. No ANSI colors ever (even on a TTY); error exit code is 1; captured text is inserted
321	    literally and is never re-scanned for `$` or `\` sequences.

1	# sd 1.0.0 — `-f/--flags` regex flag semantics (black-box probing report)
2	
3	Binary probed: `/workspace/executable` (sd 1.0.0). All probes use stdin → stdout mode.
4	Documented flags (from `gen/sd.1`): `c` case-sensitive, `e` disable multi-line matching,
5	`i` case-insensitive, `m` multi-line matching, `s` make `.` match newlines, `w` match full words only.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Executive summary of the behavioral model
10	
11	The flags are NOT independent toggles. The observed behavior is exactly reproduced by:
12	
13	1. Start with defaults: `case_insensitive = false`, `multi_line = true`, `dot_matches_new_line = false`.
14	2. Process the flag string left to right. `c`/`i` and `s` take effect **sequentially** at their
15	   position. **`w` is a reset point**: at each `w`, the pattern is wrapped and ALL flags set so far
16	   (`i`/`c`/`s`) are discarded; flags appearing *after* the last `w` apply to the wrapped pattern.
17	3. `m`/`e` are **not** sequential — they act like position-independent post-checks on the whole
18	   flag string:
19	   - `multi_line = false` if `e` appears anywhere, OR if `s` appears anywhere and `m` does not.
20	   - `multi_line = false` unconditionally if `w` appears anywhere (even `-f wm` / `-f mw` — `m`
21	     can never re-enable multi-line once `w` is present).
22	   - otherwise `multi_line = true` (the default).
23	4. `dot_matches_new_line = true` iff `s` appears (after the last `w`, if `w` is present).
24	5. `case_insensitive = true` iff the last of `c`/`i` (after the last `w`, if `w` is present) is `i`.
25	6. `w` wraps the pattern as literally `\b` + PATTERN + `\b` — **no grouping** (see §5).
26	
27	Equivalent pseudo-code that matches every observation:
28	
29	```
30	fn compile(pattern, flags: Option<String>) -> Regex {
31	    let mut rb = RegexBuilder::new(pattern);
32	    rb.multi_line(true);
33	    if let Some(f) = flags {
34	        for c in f.chars() {           // sequential pass
35	            match c {
36	                'c' => rb.case_insensitive(false),
37	                'i' => rb.case_insensitive(true),
38	                's' => rb.dot_matches_new_line(true),
39	                'w' => rb = RegexBuilder::new(&format!(r"\b{}\b", pattern)), // fresh builder: all defaults off
40	                _   => {}              // 'm', 'e', and ANY unknown char: no-op here
41	            }
42	        }
43	        // position-independent post-checks on the original flag string:
44	        if f.contains('e') || (f.contains('s') && !f.contains('m')) {
45	            rb.multi_line(false);
46	        }
47	    }
48	    rb.build()
49	}
50	```
51	
52	(The exact internal structure can't be known black-box, but this reproduces 100% of the probed
53	behavior, including all order-dependence quirks below.)
54	
55	---
56	
57	## 2. `i` / `c` — case sensitivity
58	
59	Default is case-sensitive. `i` enables case-insensitive (Unicode-aware simple folding: `CAFÉ`
60	matches `café`). `c` disables it.
61	
62	**`c` and `i` are order-dependent: the LAST one in the flag string wins.** (`c` is NOT a blanket
63	override of `i`.)
64	
65	```
66	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable 'foo' 'X'          → Foo FOO X      (default: sensitive)
67	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f i 'foo' 'X'     → X X X
68	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f c 'foo' 'X'     → Foo FOO X
69	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable --flags i 'foo' 'X' → X X X         (long form works)
70	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable --flags=i 'foo' 'X' → X X X         (=form works)
71	$ printf 'Foo FOO foo\n' | ./executable -fi 'foo' 'X'       → X X X         (attached short form works)
72	
73	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f ci 'foo' 'X'   → X X      (i last → insensitive)
74	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f ic 'foo' 'X'   → FOO X    (c last → sensitive)
75	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f cic 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X
76	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f ici 'foo' 'X'  → X X
77	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f ii 'foo' 'X'   → X X      (duplicates fine)
78	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f cc 'foo' 'X'   → FOO X
79	```
80	
81	Interleaving with other flags doesn't change last-wins:
82	
83	```
84	-f icm → sensitive    -f mci → insensitive    -f mic → sensitive    -f cmi → insensitive
85	```
86	
87	Unicode folding probe:
88	
89	```
90	$ printf 'CAFÉ café\n' | ./executable -f i 'café' 'X'   → X X        (é/É fold)
91	$ printf 'CAFÉ café\n' | ./executable -f wi 'café' 'X'  → X X
92	```
93	
94	---
95	
96	## 3. `m` / `e` — multi-line anchors (`^`/`$`)
97	
98	**Default: multi-line is ON** — `^` matches at start of input and after every `\n`; `$` matches
99	before every `\n` and at end of input.
100	
101	```
102	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable '^def' 'X'   → abc\nX\n      (default: ^ matches line starts)
103	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable 'abc$' 'X'   → X\ndef\n
104	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable 'def$' 'X'   → abc\nX\n      ($ matches before final \n)
105	$ printf 'a\nb\n'     | ./executable '^' 'X'      → Xa\nXb\nX     (^ matches at 0, after each \n, and at end pos 4)
106	```
107	
108	`e` disables multi-line: `^` = absolute start of input only, `$` = absolute end of input only
109	(NOTE: with `e`, `$` does NOT match before a trailing final newline):
110	
111	```
112	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f e '^def' 'X'  → abc\ndef\n   (no match)
113	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f e '^abc' 'X'  → X\ndef\n     (^ still matches pos 0)
114	$ printf 'abc\ndef'   | ./executable -f e 'def$' 'X'  → abc\nX       ($ at true end)
115	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f e 'def$' 'X'  → abc\ndef\n   (NO match — $ ≠ before trailing \n)
116	$ printf 'a\nb\n'     | ./executable -f e '^' 'X'     → Xa\nb\n      (only pos 0)
117	```
118	
119	`m` = multi-line on (same as default; only observable in combinations, below).
120	
121	**`e` beats `m` regardless of order** (position-independent):
122	
123	```
124	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f me '^c' 'X'   → unchanged
125	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f em '^c' 'X'   → unchanged
126	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f m  '^c' 'X'   → abc\nXd
127	```
128	
129	`e` does NOT affect anything else: literal `\n` in the pattern still matches newlines, `.` still
130	does not match `\n`:
131	
132	```
133	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f e 'c\nd' 'X'  → abXef\n
134	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f e 'c.d' 'X'   → unchanged
135	```
136

138	
139	## 4. `s` — dot matches newline; SIDE EFFECT: disables multi-line unless `m` also present
140	
141	`-f s` makes `.` match `\n`:
142	
143	```
144	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable 'c.d' 'X'      → unchanged      (default: . excludes \n)
145	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f s 'c.d' 'X' → abXef\n
146	$ printf 'abc\ndef\n' | ./executable -f s 'a.*f' 'X' → X\n           (.* swallows the \n)
147	```
148	
149	**Surprising side effect: `s` alone also turns multi-line OFF** (both `^` and `$` affected):
150	
151	```
152	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n'   | ./executable -f s '^c' 'X'   → unchanged    (no line-start match!)
153	$ printf 'abc\nc\nd\n' | ./executable -f s 'c$' 'X'   → unchanged    (no line-end match!)
154	$ printf 'abc\nc\nd\n' | ./executable -f s 'c.d' 'X'  → abc\nX\n     (dotall itself works)
155	$ printf 'a\nb\n'      | ./executable -f s '^' 'X'    → Xa\nb\n      (only pos 0)
156	```
157	
158	…but if `m` appears **anywhere** in the same flag string, multi-line stays ON — **order does not
159	matter** (`sm` and `ms` identical), unlike `c`/`i`:
160	
161	```
162	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n'   | ./executable -f sm '^c' 'X'   → abc\nXd
163	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n'   | ./executable -f ms '^c' 'X'   → abc\nXd
164	$ printf 'abc\nc\nd\n' | ./executable -f sm '^c.d' 'X' → abc\nX\n    (ml + dotall together)
165	$ printf 'a\nb\n'      | ./executable -f sm '^' 'X'    → Xa\nXb\nX
166	```
167	
168	More confirmations of the "post-check" nature (`e` always wins; `s` kills ml unless `m` present):
169	
170	```
171	-f sme, -f sem, -f esm, -f ems, -f mes, -f mse   → all ml OFF (e present)
172	-f ss   → ml off, dotall on (duplicates fine)
173	-f mm   → ml on
174	-f ee   → ml off
175	-f sim, -f mis, -f ims → ml on, ci on, dotall on
176	-f si, -f is, -f sc, -f cs → ml off
177	-f sxm  → ml on + dotall on (unknown char x ignored, see §7)
178	```
179	
180	So: `multi_line = !contains('e') && (!contains('s') || contains('m'))` (when no `w`; see §5/§6).
181

183	
184	## 5. `w` — full-word matching: the pattern is wrapped as `\b` + PATTERN + `\b` (NOT grouped!)
185	
186	Basic behavior — only matches at Unicode word boundaries (`\b`); digits and `_` are word chars,
187	punctuation/space are not, Unicode letters (é, α) are word chars:
188	
189	```
190	$ printf 'foo_bar bar1 1bar bar, bar\n' | ./executable -f w 'bar' 'X'  → foo_bar bar1 1bar X, X
191	$ printf 'a-b a.b a_b\n'  | ./executable -f w 'a' 'X'   → X-b X.b a_b
192	$ printf 'a-b a.b a_b\n'  | ./executable -f w 'b' 'X'   → a-X a.X a_b
193	$ printf 'café naïve café\n' | ./executable -f w 'café' 'X' → X naïve X
194	$ printf 'café\n'         | ./executable -f w 'fé' 'X'  → unchanged   (no boundary inside word)
195	$ printf 'αβγ α βγ\n'     | ./executable -f w 'α' 'X'   → αβγ X βγ
196	$ printf 'cafeé é\n'      | ./executable -f w 'é' 'X'   → cafeé X
197	```
198	
199	### 5.1 The wrap is exactly `\bPATTERN\b` — no non-capturing group
200	
201	Discriminator probes with alternation:
202	
203	```
204	$ printf 'ax bx\n' | ./executable -f w 'a|b' 'X'     → Xx bx
205	$ printf 'ab x\n'  | ./executable -f w 'a|ab' 'X'    → Xb x        ('a' matched, leaving 'b'!)
206	$ printf 'xcd ab\n' | ./executable -f w 'ab|cd' 'X'  → xX X        ('cd' matched INSIDE 'xcd'!)
207	```
208	
209	With a grouped wrap `\b(?:a|b)\b`, none of these would match ('a' in 'ax'/'ab' fails the trailing
210	`\b`; 'cd' in 'xcd' fails the leading `\b`). With the naive wrap `\ba|b\b` = `(\ba)|(b\b)`:
211	`\ba` matches 'a' at pos 0 of 'ax'/'ab' (no trailing boundary required on that alternative), and
212	`cd\b` matches 'cd' in 'xcd' (no leading boundary on that alternative). Exactly as observed.
213	
214	Direct confirmation from the error message for an invalid pattern — the wrapped pattern is echoed:
215	
216	```
217	$ printf 'x\n' | ./executable -f w '(' 'X'
218	exit=1, stdout empty, stderr exactly:
219	error: invalid regex regex parse error:\n    \b(\b\n      ^\nerror: unclosed group\n
220	```
221	
222	i.e. the pattern literally became `\b(\b`.
223	
224	Consequences for reimplementation:
225	- Alternation, anchors, and groups inside the pattern are NOT protected from the glued-on `\b`s.
226	- Capture-group numbering is unaffected (the wrap adds no groups):
227	  `printf 'x ab y zab\n' | ./executable -f w '(a)(b)' '$2$1'` → `x ba y zab`.
228	- Patterns ending/starting with non-word chars interact with the glued `\b` naively:
229	
230	```
231	$ printf 'a!5 a! a!_\n' | ./executable -f w 'a!' 'X'   → X5 a! X_
232	      ('a!' before space/newline does NOT match: no \b between '!' and non-word;
233	       'a!' before '5'/'_' DOES match: \b exists between '!' and word char)
234	$ printf '!a x!a !a5\n' | ./executable -f w '!a' 'X'   → !a xX !a5
235	      ('x!a' matches: \b exists between word 'x' and non-word '!';
236	       leading-'!a' and after-space '!a' do NOT match: no \b before '!';
237	       '!a5' fails trailing \b)
238	$ printf 'ab\n' | ./executable -f w 'x*' 'Y' | od -c   → Y a b Y \n
239	      (empty-matching pattern: `\bx*\b` matches empty at pos 0 and pos 2 — the two
240	       positions where \b holds — standard leftmost empty-match iteration)
241	```
242	
243	### 5.2 `w` forces multi-line OFF — unconditionally
244	
245	Anchors with `w` only work at the absolute start/end of input, and `m` cannot re-enable it:
246	
247	```
248	$ printf 'cd\n'      | ./executable -f w '^cd' 'X'   → X\n          (^ ok at pos 0: \b^cd\b)
249	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f w '^cd' 'X'   → unchanged    (no line-2 match)
250	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f mw '^cd' 'X'  → unchanged    (m does NOT help!)
251	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f wm '^cd' 'X'  → unchanged    (order doesn't matter either)
252	$ printf 'a cd\nzz\n' | ./executable -f w 'cd$' 'X'  → unchanged
253	$ printf 'a cd\nzz\n' | ./executable -f wm 'cd$' 'X' → unchanged
254	$ printf 'x a'       | ./executable -f w 'a$' 'X'    → x X          ($ at true end works)
255	$ printf 'x a\n'     | ./executable -f w 'a$' 'X'    → unchanged    ($ before \n fails — ml off)
256	```
257	
258	Exhaustive check, `^cd` on `abc\ncd\n` — ALL of these gave no match (ml off):
259	`w, wm, mw, wsm, wms, mws, smw, msw, wme, wem, ewm`.
260	
261	Literal `\n` in a `w` pattern still works: `printf 'a cd\nzz\n' | ./executable -f w 'cd\n' 'X'`
262	→ `a Xzz\n` (wrap `\bcd\n\b`: after `\n` comes word char 'z' → trailing `\b` holds).
263	
264	### 5.3 `w` wipes previously-set flags; flags after the last `w` still apply
265	
266	Case-insensitivity:
267	
268	```
269	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f iw 'foo' 'X'   → FOO X    (i BEFORE w: lost → sensitive!)
270	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f wi 'foo' 'X'   → X X      (i after w: applies)
271	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f wic 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X    (after w: i then c → c wins)
272	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f wci 'foo' 'X'  → X X      (after w: c then i → i wins)
273	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f ciw 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X    (both before w → lost)
274	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f wiw 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X    (i before LAST w → lost)
275	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f iwi 'foo' 'X'  → X X      (i after last w → applies)
276	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f iww 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X
277	$ printf 'FOO foo\n' | ./executable -f wwi 'foo' 'X'  → X X
278	```
279	
280	Dot-all (`s`):
281	
282	```
283	input 'ab c\nd e\n', pattern 'c.d':
284	-f s   → match (ab X e)        -f sw  → no match (s before w: lost)
285	-f ws  → match                 -f wsw → no match (s before last w: lost)
286	-f wss → match                 -f ssw → no match
287	-f wsm → match                 -f wms → match    (s after w applies; ml still off — irrelevant here)
288	-f smw → no match              -f msw → no match
289	```
290	
291	So the "reset point" is the LAST `w` in the string: `c`/`i`/`s` before it are discarded, those
292	after it apply. Multi-line is off whenever any `w` is present, period (§5.2).
293	
294	`w` duplicates are harmless (`-f ww` behaves like `-f w`; wrap is idempotent in effect since
295	`\b\bfoo\b\b` ≡ `\bfoo\b`):
296	
297	```
298	$ printf 'x foo y xfoo\n' | ./executable -f ww 'foo' 'X'  → x X y xfoo
299	```

331	## 7. Invalid, empty, duplicate, and repeated flags
332	
333	**Unknown flag characters are SILENTLY IGNORED** — no error, no warning, exit code 0, replacement
334	proceeds normally. Verified for `x`, `d`, `1`, `I` (uppercase), `W` (uppercase), `u`, ` ` (space),
335	`-`, `é` (multibyte UTF-8):
336	
337	```
338	$ printf 'foo\n' | ./executable -f x 'foo' 'X'    → X      exit=0, stderr empty
339	$ printf 'foo\n' | ./executable -f 'I' 'foo' 'X'  → X      exit=0  (uppercase I is NOT i!)
340	$ printf 'foo\n' | ./executable -f 'é' 'foo' 'X'  → X      exit=0
341	```
342	
343	Known flags mixed with unknown chars still apply normally:
344	
345	```
346	$ printf 'FOO foo xfoo\n' | ./executable -f ix 'foo' 'X'    → X X xX     (i applies)
347	$ printf 'FOO foo xfoo\n' | ./executable -f xw 'foo' 'X'    → FOO X xfoo (w applies)
348	$ printf 'FOO foo xfoo\n' | ./executable -f qiwz 'foo' 'X'  → FOO X xfoo (i before w lost, w applies)
349	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n'      | ./executable -f xe '^cd' 'X'    → unchanged  (e applies)
350	```
351	
352	**Empty flag string** `-f ''`: accepted, behaves exactly like no `-f` at all (multi-line ON default):
353	
354	```
355	$ printf 'foo\n' | ./executable -f '' 'foo' 'X'          → X     exit=0
356	$ printf 'abc\ncd\n' | ./executable -f '' '^cd' 'X'      → abc\nXd
357	```
358	
359	**Duplicates** are fine: `ii`, `cc`, `ss`, `mm`, `ee`, `ww`, `sxs` all accepted with expected
360	semantics.
361	
362	**Repeating the `-f` option itself is a hard clap error** (exit code 2, stdout empty). Exact stderr
363	bytes (note: program name is taken from argv[0] basename — here `executable`):
364	
365	```
366	$ printf 'FOO\n' | ./executable -f i -f c 'foo' 'X'
367	exit=2
368	stderr:
369	error: the argument '--flags <FLAGS>' cannot be used multiple times\n
370	\n
371	Usage: executable [OPTIONS] <FIND> <REPLACE_WITH> [FILES]...\n
372	\n
373	For more information, try '--help'.\n
374	```
375	
376	(same for `-f c -f i`, `--flags i --flags c`, etc.)
377	
378	**Invalid regex after wrapping**: exit code 1, stdout empty, stderr (exact bytes):
379	
380	```
381	$ printf 'x\n' | ./executable -f w '(' 'X'
382	exit=1
383	stderr: error: invalid regex regex parse error:\n    \b(\b\n      ^\nerror: unclosed group\n
384	```
385	
386	Baseline without flags (`-f` omitted, pattern `(`): same shape, pattern shown unwrapped:
387	
388	```
389	exit=1
390	stderr: error: invalid regex regex parse error:\n    (\n    ^\nerror: unclosed group\n
391	```

395	## 8. Misc
396	
397	- `-f` works identically in long form (`--flags i`, `--flags=i`) and attached short form (`-fi`).
398	- `-f` composes with `-F` (fixed-strings): the `w` wrap is applied around the (escaped) literal:
399	  `printf 'xfoo foo\n' | ./executable -F -f w 'foo' 'X'` → `xfoo X`;
400	  `printf 'f.o foo\n' | ./executable -f w -F 'f.o' 'X'` → `X foo` (literal `f.o` word-matched).
401	- All flag processing is per-run on the whole input (stdin treated as one string); exit code for
402	  successful replacements is 0 whether or not anything matched.

405	
406	## 9. 10-line summary of the most surprising/important findings
407	
408	1. The `w` wrap is literally `\b` + PATTERN + `\b` with NO grouping — `-f w 'ab|cd'` matches `cd` inside `xcd`, and `-f w 'a|ab'` replaces just the `a` of `ab`.
409	2. This is directly confirmed by the invalid-regex error, which echoes the wrapped pattern: `error: invalid regex regex parse error:\n    \b(\b\n      ^\nerror: unclosed group\n` (exit 1).
410	3. `w` unconditionally disables multi-line (`^`/`$` only match absolute input start/end) — even `-f wm`/`-f mw` cannot re-enable it.
411	4. `w` is a reset point: `i`/`c`/`s` appearing BEFORE the last `w` are silently discarded (`-f iw` is case-sensitive!); flags after the last `w` apply normally (`-f wi` insensitive, `-f ws` dot-all).
412	5. `s` has a hidden side effect: used without `m`, it disables multi-line too (`-f s '^c'` won't match line starts); `-f sm`/`-f ms` keep it on — order-independent.
413	6. `c`/`i` ARE order-dependent, last-one-wins (`-f ci` insensitive, `-f ic` sensitive) — the opposite of the order-independent `s`/`m` and `e`/`m` pairs.
414	7. `e` always beats `m` regardless of order (`-f me` and `-f em` both disable multi-line); effective rule: `ml = !has('e') && (!has('s') || has('m')) && !has('w')`.
415	8. Unknown/invalid flag characters (`x`, `1`, `I`, `é`, space, …) are silently IGNORED — exit 0, no error at all; uppercase `I`/`W` do nothing.
416	9. Empty `-f ''` is accepted and equals the defaults (multi-line ON, case-sensitive, dot excludes `\n`); duplicate chars (`-f ii`) are fine, but repeating the option (`-f i -f c`) is a clap error, exit 2: `error: the argument '--flags <FLAGS>' cannot be used multiple times`.
417	10. Defaults: multi-line ON (`^` matches after every `\n` and even at the position after a trailing `\n`; `$` before every `\n`), case-sensitive, `.` excludes `\n`; with `-f e`, `$` does NOT match before a trailing final newline (absolute end only).

1	# sd regex-syntax — black-box probing report
2	
3	Target: `/workspace/executable` (sd v1.0.0 reimplementation target).
4	Method: black-box only — fed patterns via `printf 'input' | /workspace/executable 'PATTERN' 'REPL'`, captured exact stdout/stderr bytes (`od -c`) and exit codes. No inspection of the binary.
5	
6	Unless noted otherwise, the invocation shape for every finding below is:
7	
8	```
9	printf '%s' '<input>' | /workspace/executable '<pattern>' '<repl>' ; echo $?
10	```
11	
12	(stdin mode, no file arguments). A helper script `/workspace/probe/probe.sh` was used that
13	prints input/pattern/replacement with `%q`, exit code, stdout, and both raw and `od -c` stderr.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Engine profile (inferred from behavior)
18	
19	- The engine is a **bytes-oriented, Unicode-aware regex engine** (behaviorally identical to Rust
20	  `regex::bytes::Regex` with default options **plus multi-line mode enabled**):
21	  - `\w \d \s \b` are Unicode-aware: `\w+` matches `café１２` as one run; `\d+` matches fullwidth
22	    digits `１２`; `\s` matches U+00A0.
23	  - `.` matches one **codepoint** (not byte) but never `\n` by default, and does **not** match
24	    invalid UTF-8 bytes: `printf 'a\xffb' | sd '.' 'X'` → bytes `X 377 X` (the raw `0xFF` survived).
25	  - `\xFF` **does** match the raw byte `0xFF` (bytes-mode regex; a Unicode-scalar-only engine
26	    would reject `\xFF` as "can match invalid UTF-8").
27	- **`^` and `$` are multi-line by default** (as if `(?m)` were on):
28	  - `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd '^b' 'X'` → `a\nX\n` (exit 0)
29	  - `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd 'a$' 'X'` → `X\nb\n`
30	  - `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd '(?-m)^b' 'X'` → unchanged `a\nb\n` (multi-line can be disabled)
31	  - `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd '(?m:^)' 'X'` → `Xa\nXb\nX` (matches at start and after every `\n`, incl. trailing)
32	- `\A` = absolute start only, `\z` = absolute end only (NOT before a trailing newline):
33	  - `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd 'b\z' 'X'` → unchanged; `printf 'a\nb\n' | sd 'b\n\z' 'X'` → `a\nX`.
34	- `\b`/`\B` are standard Unicode word boundaries (`\bfoo\b` on `foo bar` → `X bar`; `\Boo` on `foobar` → `fXbar`).
35	
36	## 2. Character classes
37	
38	All supported, leftmost-match semantics:
39	
40	| command (input `abc123`, repl `X`) | stdout |
41	|---|---|
42	| `sd '[abc]'` | `XXX123` |
43	| `sd '[a-c]'` (range) | `XXX123` |
44	| `sd '[^abc]'` (negation) | `abcXXX` |
45	
46	- `.` inside a class is literal: `[a-z.]` on `a-z.` → `X-XX`.
47	- `]` as first class char is literal: `[]a-]` on `b-]` → `bXX` (matched `]` and `-`).
48	- **Nested classes / unions**: `[a-z[:digit:]_]` on `a1_` → `XXX`.
49	- **POSIX classes**: `[[:alpha:]]`, `[[:digit:]]+`, negated `[[:^digit:]]` all work.
50	  - On `Hello World 42`: `[[:alpha:]]` → `XXXXX XXXXX 42`; `[[:digit:]]+` → `Hello World N`;
51	    `[[:^digit:]]` on `ab1` → `XX1`.
52	  - An **unknown** POSIX-ish name is NOT an error: `[[:foo:]]` parses as an outer class containing
53	    the *nested* class `[:foo:]` (chars `:`,`f`,`o`) — on input `of:[]` it gives `XXX[]` (matched `o`,`f`,`:`).
54	- **Class set operations** all work:
55	  - intersection `[a-c&&b]` on `abcxy` → `aXcxy` (only `b`)
56	  - difference `[a-c--b]` on `abcxy` → `XbXxy` (`a`,`c`)
57	  - symmetric difference `[a-c~~b]` on `abcxy` → `XbXxy` (`a`,`c`)
58	- Negated classes match `\n`: `printf 'x\ny' | sd '[^x]' 'M'` → bytes `x M M`.
59	- Empty class `[]` and `[^]` are **errors** (unclosed character class — see §7).
60	
61	## 3. Escape sequences
62	
63	Supported (verified by matching):
64	
65	| escape | meaning / probe result |
66	|---|---|
67	| `\d \D \w \W \s \S` | Unicode-aware; all work (see §1) |
68	| `\b \B` | word / non-word boundary (assertions) |
69	| `\A \z` | absolute start / end of haystack |
70	| `\n \t \r \f \v` | LF, TAB, CR, FF, VT — all matched the literal control chars |
71	| `\a` | bell (0x07) — valid escape (no match in `ab`, no error) |
72	| `\x41` | 2-hex-digit: matched `A` |
73	| `\xFF` | matches raw byte 0xFF (bytes mode) |
74	| `\x{263A}` | matched `☺` (U+263A) |
75	| `\u0041`, `\u{41}` | BOTH accepted, matched `A` |
76	| `\p{L}+`, `\pL+` | Unicode property classes; on `héllo1` → `X1` |
77	| `\b{start}` | supported (new-style boundary); on `ab` → `Xab` |
78	| `\b{end}` | supported; `a\b{end}` on `ab` → no match (correct) |
79	| `\.` `\*` etc. | escaped punctuation = literal; `\.` on `a.b` → `aXb`; `\*` on `a*b` → `aXb` |
80	
81	NOT supported (all exit 1, error text in §7):
82	
83	- `\0` and `\1`..`\9`, `\101` (octal-looking) → **"backreferences are not supported"**
84	  (caret spans only the first two chars `\1` of `\101`)
85	- `\k<n>` (named backref) → "unrecognized escape sequence"
86	- `\e`, `\K`, `\G`, `\Z`, `\h`, `\C`, `\q` → "unrecognized escape sequence"
87	- `\U0041` → "incomplete escape sequence, reached end of pattern prematurely" (caret at end, past `\U`)
88	- `[\b]` → "invalid escape sequence found in character class" (caret on the `\b` inside class)
89	- `\x` at end → "incomplete escape sequence, reached end of pattern prematurely"
90	- `\xZZ` → "invalid hexadecimal digit" (caret under first `Z`)
91	- `\x{}` → "hexadecimal literal empty" (carets `^^` under `{}`)
92	- `\x{110000}` → "hexadecimal literal is not a Unicode scalar value" (carets under `110000`)
93	- `\p{Foo}` → "Unicode property not found" (carets span whole `\p{Foo}`)
94	- trailing backslash `a\` → "incomplete escape sequence, reached end of pattern prematurely" (caret after `\`)
95	
96	## 4. Repetition
97	
98	All standard quantifiers work, greedy by default; all lazy forms work:
99	
100	| input | pattern | stdout (repl `X`) |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| `aaa` | `a*` | `X` |
103	| `aaa` | `a+` | `X` |
104	| `aaa` | `a?` | `XXX` |
105	| `aaaa` | `a{2}` | `XX` |
106	| `aaaa` | `a{2,}` | `X` |
107	| `aaaaa` | `a{2,3}` | `XX` |
108	| `aaaa` | `a{2,10}` | `X` |
109	| `aaa` | `a*?` | `XaXaXaX` (lazy: empty matches everywhere) |
110	| `aaa` | `a+?` | `XXX` |
111	| `ab` | `ab??` | `Xb` |
112	| `aaaa` | `a{1,3}?` | `XXXX` |
113	
114	- Stacked quantifier `a**` is **accepted** (parses as `(a*)*`): on `abc` → `XbXcX`.
115	- Repetition on groups works: `(ab){2}` etc. (no surprises).
116	- Count limits: `a{99999999999}` and `a{4294967296}` → parse error "decimal literal invalid",
117	  carets under the digits (after `a{`); see §7.
118	
119	### Empty-match rule (important for reimplementation)
120	
121	`sd` replaces **all non-overlapping matches**, but an **empty match that starts exactly where the
122	previous match ended is skipped** (classic `find_iter` empty-match bump behavior):
123	
124	| input | pattern | stdout (repl `M`) |
125	|---|---|---|
126	| `ab` | `x*` | `MaMbM` |
127	| `ab` | `` (empty pattern) | `MaMbM` |
128	| `aab` | `a*` | `MbM` (match `aa`, skip empty@2, keep empty@3) |
129	| `ab` | `a?` | `MbM` |
130	| `aba` | `a*` | `MbM` |
131	| `ab` | `a\|` | `MbM` |
132	| `ab` | `\|a` | `MaMbM` (empty alternative wins leftmost at every pos) |
133	| `ab` | `a\|\|b` | `MbM` (empty 2nd alternative beats `b` at pos 1) |
134	| `ab` | `b\|` | `MaM` |
135	
136	## 5. Alternation
137	
138	- Leftmost (NOT longest) wins: `ab|abc` on `abc` → `Mc`; `abc|ab` on `abc` → `M`.
139	- Precedence: alternation is lowest — `x|ab` on `xabcy` → `MMcy`.
140	- Empty branches allowed anywhere: `a|`, `|a`, `a||b` (see table above). Exit 0.
141	
142	## 6. Groups and inline flags
143	
144	- `(...)`, `(?:...)`, `(?P<name>...)`, `(?<name>...)`: all supported. Named groups usable in
145	  replacement via `$name`: `(?P<g>ab)c` on `abc` with `[$g]` → `[ab]`; `(?:ab)c` leaves `$1` empty → `[]`.
146	- Group names: `[A-Za-z0-9_]`-ish, must not start with digit: `(?P<_a>x)` OK; `(?P<1a>x)` and
147	  `(?<na-me>x)` → error "invalid capture group character" (caret at first bad char).
148	- Inline flags `(?i)`, `(?i:...)`, `(?-i:...)`, `(?s:.)`, `(?m:^)`, `(?x)`, `(?u)`, `(?R)` all work:
149	  - `(?i)abc` on `AbC` → `X`
150	  - Flags apply from their position onward: `a(?i)bc` on `AbC dEf` → no match (leading `a` case-sensitive)
151	  - `(?i)(?-i:ab)c` on `AbC` → no match; `(?i)(?-i)abc` → no match
152	  - `(?s)a.b` on `a\nb\n` matches across newline; without `s`, no
153	  - `(?m:^b)` matches `b` after `\n`; note multi-line is ON by default anyway (§1), `(?-m)` turns it off
154	  - `(?x)` ignores whitespace and `#`-to-EOL comments: `(?x)a#comment` on `a#c` → `X#c`
155	  - `(?R)` (CRLF mode) accepted without error.
156	- Duplicate names (even across alternation branches) are an error:
157	  `(?P<a>x)|(?P<a>y)` → "duplicate capture group name", carets under BOTH name occurrences.
158	
159	### Unsupported constructs (all exit 1, messages verbatim in §7)
160	
161	- Backreference in pattern: `(a)\1`, bare `\1` → "backreferences are not supported"
162	- Look-ahead `(?=a)`, `(?!a)` → "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported" (carets `^^^`)
163	- Look-behind `(?<=a)`, `(?<!a)` → same message (carets `^^^^`)
164	- Atomic group `(?>a)` → "unrecognized flag" (caret under `>`)
165

346	### 7.4 Non-error cases
347	
348	- Valid pattern, no match: exit 0, input passed through unchanged.
349	- `-F`/`--fixed-strings` mode does not parse regex: `printf 'a(' | sd -F '(' 'X'` → `aX`, exit 0.

351	## 8. 10-line summary of key findings
352	
353	1. Engine behaves as Rust `regex::bytes` Unicode-aware regex: `\w\d\s\b` match full Unicode (fullwidth digits, é, NBSP), but `.` skips invalid UTF-8 bytes while `\xFF` matches raw byte 0xFF.
354	2. `^`/`$` are MULTI-LINE BY DEFAULT (like `(?m)` always on); `(?-m)` disables; `\A`/`\z` are absolute, `\z` does not allow a trailing newline.
355	3. All standard classes incl. nested/union/intersection `[a-c&&b]`, difference `--`, symdiff `~~`, and POSIX `[[:alpha:]]`/`[[:^digit:]]` work; unknown `[[:foo:]]` silently parses as a nested literal class.
356	4. All quantifiers + lazy forms work; `a**` is accepted; empty matches that start where the previous match ended are SKIPPED (`a?` on `ab` → `MbM`, not `MMbM`).
357	5. Leftmost (not longest) alternation; empty branches `a|`, `|a`, `a||b` legal; empty alternative wins leftmost.
358	6. Groups: `()`, `(?:)`, `(?P<n>)`, `(?<n>)` all OK; names `[A-Za-z0-9_]`, no leading digit, duplicates error with carets under both names.
359	7. Flags `i m s x u R` work, positional and scoped `(?i:...)`/`(?-i:...)` forms OK; `(?x)` supports `#` comments.
360	8. Unsupported: backrefs `\1`/`\0`/`\101`/`\k<n>` → "backreferences are not supported" (or "unrecognized escape" for `\k`); all lookarounds → "look-around, including look-ahead and look-behind, is not supported"; atomic `(?>` → "unrecognized flag"; also `\Z \h \C \e \K \G` rejected, but `\a \u0041 \u{41} \b{start} \b{end}` ARE supported.
361	9. Every regex error: exit 1, empty stdout, stderr = `error: invalid regex ` + verbatim engine display — `regex parse error:\n    <pattern>\n    <carets>\nerror: <msg>\n`, no ANSI codes when piped; multi-line patterns use a 79-char `~`-ruled `N: `-numbered block instead.
362	10. Non-parse errors differ: compiled-size overflow is a single line `error: invalid regex Compiled regex exceeds size limit of 10485760 bytes.`; no-match is exit 0 with input unchanged; `-F` bypasses all of this.

2	
3	Binary: `/workspace/executable` (reports `sd 1.0.0`).
4	Method: black-box only — CLI args + stdin/stdout/stderr + files. All outputs captured with `od -c`; exit codes via `$?`. Commands below are exact as run (via `bash -c` so quoting is faithful). `od -c` shows `\0` for NUL, `\n` for LF, `\r` for CR, and octal for non-ASCII bytes (e.g. `377` = 0xFF, `303 251` = UTF-8 for `é`).

9	
10	## 1. Alternation: leftmost-first, NOT longest
11	
12	Rust-regex-style semantics: the first alternative that allows an overall match wins; there is no longest-match preference.
13	
14	```
15	printf 'ab'   | /workspace/executable 'a|ab' 'X'        ->  X b        (matched just "a")
16	printf 'ab'   | /workspace/executable 'ab|a' 'X'        ->  X          (alternation order matters)
17	printf 'abcd' | /workspace/executable '(a|ab)(c|bcd)' 'X'      ->  X
18	printf 'abcd' | /workspace/executable '(a|ab)(c|bcd)' '[$1|$2]' ->  [ a | b c d ]
19	```
20	
21	`(a|ab)(c|bcd)` on `abcd` captures `$1=a`, `$2=bcd`: group 1 takes the first alternative `a` (not `ab`), then group 2 takes `bcd`. Classic leftmost-first backtracking order (as the regex crate's PikeVM/DFA simulate).
22	
23	## 2. Greedy vs lazy quantifiers
24	
25	```
26	printf 'aaa' | /workspace/executable 'a+'  '-'   ->  -            (one greedy match of all 3)
27	printf 'aaa' | /workspace/executable 'a+?' '-'   ->  - - -        (three 1-char lazy matches)
28	printf 'aaa' | /workspace/executable 'a*'  '-'   ->  -            (greedy; note: NO trailing empty-match replacement, see §3)
29	printf 'aaa' | /workspace/executable 'a*?' '-'   ->  - a - a - a -  (lazy empty matches at every position incl. end)
30	```
31	
32	Both `+?` and `*?` lazy forms are supported.
33	
34	## 3. Empty-match handling and advancing
35	
36	Advancing rule (matches Rust `regex` crate `find_iter`/`replace_all` exactly):
37	
38	- An empty match at position *i* is replaced, then the scan position advances by **one character** (that char is copied verbatim).
39	- An empty match that starts **exactly where the previous match ended** is **skipped** (not replaced); scanning then advances one char.
40	- The empty match at the very end of input **is** replaced, provided it doesn't collide with the previous match's end.
41	
42	Evidence:
43	
44	```
45	printf 'ab'  | /workspace/executable 'x*' '-'    ->  - a - b -     (empty matches at 0,1,2 all replaced)
46	printf 'axb' | /workspace/executable 'x*' '-'    ->  - a - b -     (empty@0, real match "x"@1–2,
47	                                                                    empty@2 SKIPPED since prev match ended at 2,
48	                                                                    'b' copied, empty@3 replaced)
49	printf 'ab'  | /workspace/executable '' '-'      ->  - a - b -     (empty pattern = empty match everywhere)
50	printf 'aaa' | /workspace/executable 'a*' '-'    ->  -             (match 0–3, then empty@3 skipped: it coincides
51	                                                                    with previous match end at end-of-input)
52	```
53	
54	Compare with `a*?` on `aaa` → `-a-a-a-`: there each previous match is empty at *i*, scan advances to *i+1*, so the next empty match at *i+1* is legal; final empty at 3 is legal because prev match ended at 2.
55	
56	### `-n` (max replacements) counts empty matches
57	
58	```
59	printf 'ab' | /workspace/executable -n 1 'x*' '-'  ->  - a b
60	printf 'ab' | /workspace/executable -n 2 'x*' '-'  ->  - a - b
61	```
62	
63	## 4. `^` / `$` — MULTI-LINE IS ON BY DEFAULT (no flags needed)
64	
65	The whole input (stdin or file) is treated as ONE buffer; `^`/`$` are multi-line by default. `-f e` disables multi-line; `-f m` explicitly enables it (same as default).
66	
67	```
68	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '^' '>'       ->  > a \n > b \n >     (positions 0, after \n, AND at end-of-buffer after trailing \n)
69	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '$' '<'       ->  a < \n b < \n <     (before each \n AND at very end)
70	printf 'ab'     | /workspace/executable '$' '<'       ->  a b <               (end-of-buffer, no newline)
71	printf 'ab\n'   | /workspace/executable '$' '<'       ->  a b < \n <          (BOTH before trailing \n AND at very end — two matches!)
72	printf 'ab\n'   | /workspace/executable '^' '>'       ->  > a b \n >          (start-of-buffer AND position after trailing \n)
73	printf ''       | /workspace/executable '^' '>'       ->  >
74	printf ''       | /workspace/executable '$' '<'       ->  <
75	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable -f e '^' '>'  ->  > a \n b \n         (only position 0)
76	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable -f e '$' '<'  ->  a \n b \n <         (only very end)
77	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable -f m '^' '>'  ->  > a \n > b \n >     (identical to default)
78	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '\A' '>'      ->  > a \n b \n         (\A = buffer start only)
79	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '\z' '<'      ->  a \n b \n <         (\z = buffer end only)
80	printf 'ab\n'   | /workspace/executable 'b$' 'X'      ->  a X \n
81	printf 'ab'     | /workspace/executable 'b$' 'X'      ->  a X
82	```
83	
84	**Key spec point:** in default mode `$` on input ending with `\n` produces TWO matches (before the `\n`, and at end-of-buffer). Same for `^` after a trailing `\n`. `\A`/`\z` are supported and anchor to buffer boundaries only.
85	
86	## 5. `.` and newlines; `\n` in patterns; cross-line matching
87	
88	- Default: `.` does NOT match `\n`, but DOES match `\r` and even NUL (`\0`).
89	- `-f s`: `.` matches `\n` too.
90	- `\n` in the pattern matches a literal newline in the input — input is one buffer, not line-by-line.
91	- Patterns can span newlines whenever the pattern itself contains `\n` or a `-f s`-enabled `.`.
92	
93	```
94	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '.' 'X'          ->  X \n X \n
95	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable -f s '.' 'X'     ->  X X X X        (all 4 bytes incl. both \n)
96	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable '\n' ','         ->  a , b ,
97	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable 'a.b' 'X'        ->  a \n b \n      (no match without -f s)
98	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable -f s 'a.b' 'X'   ->  X \n
99	printf 'a\nb\n' | /workspace/executable 'a\nb' 'X'       ->  X \n           (multi-line pattern, no flags needed)
100	printf 'a\nb'   | /workspace/executable '\s' '-'         ->  a - b          (\s matches \n)
101	```
102	
103	## 6. CRLF handling
104	
105	No special CRLF treatment: `\r` is an ordinary character. `$` matches only before `\n` (so it lands AFTER the `\r`), never before `\r`.
106	
107	```
108	printf 'a\r\nb\r\n' | /workspace/executable '$' '<'    ->  a \r < \n b \r < \n <
109	printf 'a\r\nb\r\n' | /workspace/executable '.' 'X'    ->  X X \n X X \n      (. matches \r, not \n)
110	printf 'a\r\nb\r\n' | /workspace/executable '\r\n' '|' ->  a | b |
111	printf 'a\r\nb\r\n' | /workspace/executable '\r$' '<'  ->  a < \n b < \n
112	```
113	
114	## 7. NUL bytes
115	
116	Fully transparent — treated as ordinary bytes/chars, no error, no truncation:
117	
118	```
119	printf 'a\0b' | /workspace/executable 'b' 'X'    ->  a \0 X
120	printf 'a\0b' | /workspace/executable 'a.b' 'X'  ->  X          (. matches NUL)
121	printf 'a\0b' | /workspace/executable '.' 'X'    ->  X X X
122	```
123	
124	## 8. Invalid UTF-8 in input
125	
126	No error, no panic — exit 0, and **invalid bytes pass through unchanged**. `.` (even `(?s).`) does NOT match invalid bytes (Unicode-aware `.` skips them), but literal patterns around them still work:
127	
128	```
129	printf '\xff\xfe' | /workspace/executable 'x' 'y'     ->  377 376          (unchanged, exit 0)
130	printf '\xff\xfe' | /workspace/executable '.' 'y'     ->  377 376          (. does not match them)
131	printf '\xff\xfe' | /workspace/executable '(?s).' 'y' ->  377 376          (not even with dotall)
132	printf 'a\xffb'   | /workspace/executable 'b' 'X'     ->  a 377 X
133	```
134	
135	Same behavior in file mode: `printf 'a\xffb' > f.bin; /workspace/executable 'b' 'X' f.bin` → exit 0, file becomes `a 377 X`.
136	
137	To match arbitrary bytes, disable Unicode in the pattern — this works:
138	
139	```
140	printf '\xff\xfe' | /workspace/executable '(?-u:.)' 'y' ->  y y
141	printf 'a\xffb'   | /workspace/executable '(?-u:.)' 'y' ->  y y y
142	```
143	
144	This strongly indicates the engine is the Rust `regex` crate's **bytes** API (`regex::bytes::Regex`) with Unicode mode on by default.
